slides.title: The token cost model
slides.text: Session 1 The token cost model Price one request from its token counts and a price sheet Explain why cached, reasoning and failed tokens change the bill Reconcile a cost model with an invoice line by line 01

slides.title: Mawj Telecom runs three applications behind one gateway
slides.text: The case study Mawj Telecom runs three applications behind one gateway Anis A bilingual care assistant. 37,974 requests in October, SAR 911. Khulasa A job that summarises calls. 25,633 tagged requests, SAR 846, and a pilot on a leased node. Fasil An agent that handles billing disputes. 3,200 sessions, SAR 2,515. All three call the provider through Maabar, the gateway, which logs one row per attempt: 97,318 rows for the month. The invoice says SAR 8,242.62. You are the cost engineer who has to explain it.

slides.title: A request costs its tokens times the price of each kind
slides.text: Recap from AE-203 A request costs its tokens times the price of each kind Tier Input Cached input Output tier-s 0.60 0.06 2.40 tier-m 3.00 0.30 12.00 tier-l 12.00 1.20 48.00 SAR per million tokens. A synthetic price sheet for the labs, not a provider's. The shape is what lasts. Output costs several times input, cached input a fraction of input, and each tier several times the one below. The figures change every few months.

slides.title: Reading a prompt and writing an answer are different work
slides.text: Why the prices differ Reading a prompt and writing an answer are different work Prefill The model reads the whole prompt in one pass. Cheap per token, and paid again on every call. Decode The model writes one token at a time, each needing a pass. Expensive per token, and it sets the latency. Cached prefix A prompt start the provider has already read is not read again. Billed at a fraction of the input price. One answer of Anis: 6,831 tokens in, 199 out, SAR 0.0229. The input side is 90% of it, because every turn resends the instructions and the policy text.

slides.title: A log row holds four kinds of token, and they overlap
slides.text: The cost model A log row holds four kinds of token, and they overlap uncached = input_tokens - cached_tokens # input INCLUDES cached cost = ( uncached * price["input"] + cached_tokens * price["cached_input"] + (output_tokens + reasoning_tokens) * price["output"] # output EXCLUDES reasoning ) / 1e6 What goes wrong. Each provider and each gateway defines these fields its own way. Read the definition before you sum a column: whether input includes cached tokens, and whether output includes reasoning tokens.

slides.title: A failed call can still be a billed call
slides.text: Retries A failed call can still be a billed call Status in the log What happened Billed? ok The answer arrived Yes timeout The client gave up; the provider had started to answer Yes: the prompt and what was written so far error The provider refused the request No October has 1,751 timeouts in the log. They cost SAR 57 and nobody received their answers.

slides.title: The naive model is 2% off, for two large reasons that cancel
slides.text: Lab 1.1 · the result The naive model is 2% off, for two large reasons that cancel Cost model SAR Against the invoice Naive: successful rows, input and output 4,870.75 +2.1% + cached input at the cached price 3,076.23 -35.5% + reasoning tokens as output 4,651.17 -2.5% + billed timeouts 4,708.59 -1.3% Close is not correct. A model that lands near the invoice because two errors cancel breaks in the month the traffic mix changes.

slides.title: A leased accelerator is paid by the hour, used or idle
slides.text: The other unit of cost A leased accelerator is paid by the hour, used or idle Khulasa's pilot leased one node for 8 hours a night: 248 hours at SAR 14, SAR 3,472 on the invoice. It served 4,500 summaries and was busy 18% of its leased time. Cost per request is the lease over the requests served. Tokens on the node have no price. 0.772 SAR per summary on the node 0.033 SAR for the same job on the API

slides.title: Reconcile by invoice line, and give the gap a name
slides.text: The evidence for this outcome Reconcile by invoice line, and give the gap a name 1 · Quantities tokens by model and kind, from the log → 2 · Lines beside each invoice line → 3 · Gap what has no row of yours Every line billed to the gateway's key matches the log token for token. The cost model gives SAR 8,180.59 against SAR 8,242.62: a gap of 0.75%, all of it on a provider key the gateway never issued.

slides.title: A model that is 1% under
slides.text: Checkpoint A model that is 1% under A colleague's cost model sums the successful rows of the log and lands 1% under the invoice in a calm month. The next month has a two-hour provider incident. What happens to the gap? It stays near 1%, because failed calls are not billed It shrinks, because fewer requests succeed It widens, because timeouts are billed and the model leaves them out It moves at random from month to month

slides.title: A cost model that matches the invoice
slides.text: Lab 1.1 · 25 min A cost model that matches the invoice Compute cost per request for the three applications and reconcile it with the synthetic invoice: from a naive model that is close for the wrong reasons to one that matches line by line, within 2% in total. D1_1_cost_model.ipynb Price one request by hand from the price sheet 5 min The month with a naive model, against the invoice 5 min Add cached tokens, reasoning tokens and billed failures 7 min Add the accelerator-hours of the pilot node 4 min Reconcile line by line and state the gap 4 min ✱ Stretch: Find the spend the gateway never saw

slides.title: Agents, retries and long contexts
slides.text: Session 2 Agents, retries and long contexts Compute cost per session from request rows Split a session into first attempts, retries, context growth and extra steps Size the saving of a step budget and of a trimmed tool result 02

slides.title: An agent's bill is counted in sessions, not in requests
slides.text: The unit of work An agent's bill is counted in sessions, not in requests 0.72 SAR, the median session of the dispute agent 11.07 SAR, its most expensive session 15x the median, in one session of 70 steps The ten most expensive sessions of October all belong to the dispute agent. An average cost per request hides every one of them.

slides.title: Every step resends everything before it
slides.text: Context growth Every step resends everything before it step 1 3,980 tokens in, none cached step 2 6,377 tokens in, 3,968 of them cached step 8 9,441 tokens in, 9,088 cached step 70 34,823 tokens in, 34,304 cached, after one billed timeout Cost grows faster than steps. Twice the steps is more than twice the cost, since each step's prompt holds all the earlier ones. In this session half of the cost came after step 44.

slides.title: An agent loop is affordable because its prefix is cached
slides.text: Cached tokens, again An agent loop is affordable because its prefix is cached The agent's month, as billed SAR 2,515 The same month with no cached token SAR 4,339 Each step's prompt starts with the previous step's prompt, so most of it is billed at the cached price. Anything that breaks that prefix, such as a new model or an edited history, is paid at the full input price.

slides.title: A retry resends the whole prompt, and an incident multiplies retries
slides.text: Retries A retry resends the whole prompt, and an incident multiplies retries The worst session made 95 attempts for 70 steps; 24 of them were billed timeouts. A client that retries at once, up to four times, turns one provider incident into several times the load. Retries are small in SAR here, 1.5% of the agent's month, and large in waiting: each timeout is a customer who waited a minute. What to configure Fewer attempts, a growing pause between them, and a circuit breaker that stops calling a provider that keeps failing.

slides.title: Split a session's bill into four parts
slides.text: Lab 1.2 · the split Split a session's bill into four parts Part What it is October, SAR Share Base the steps within a budget of 12, at the first step's prompt size 1,889.66 75.1% Context growth input beyond the first step's prompt 455.25 18.1% Extra steps steps beyond the budget 131.78 5.2% Retries billed attempts that did not succeed 38.40 1.5%

slides.title: One tool without paging fills the context for the rest of the session
slides.text: Long contexts One tool without paging fills the context for the rest of the session In 124 of 3,200 sessions a tool returned a year of itemised bills, and returned it again on later calls. Those 4% of sessions hold SAR 188 of the SAR 455 of context growth. One of them reached a prompt of 436,891 tokens in 8 steps and cost SAR 7.42. The fix is in the tool Return the three bills the dispute names, with a way to ask for more. A result the model does not need is paid for at every later step.

slides.title: Three causes, three fixes, each with its size
slides.text: Measure before optimising Three causes, three fixes, each with its size Cause Fix At stake in October The agent loops a step budget and a stop rule for "pending" SAR 131.78 A tool returns too much page and trim tool results up to SAR 188.47 Timeouts retried at once fewer attempts, a pause, a circuit breaker SAR 38.40 Size first. The fix that sounds most urgent after an incident is not always the largest. A table like this is what a cost review is made of.

slides.title: Twice the steps
slides.text: Checkpoint Twice the steps After a change to a tool, the dispute agent takes 12 steps per session where it took 6. Nothing else changed and the prefix cache still works. What happens to the cost of a session? It more than doubles, because each added step also resends a longer history It doubles, because cost is proportional to steps It barely moves, because the history is cached It stays the same, because only failed steps add cost

slides.title: The ten most expensive sessions
slides.text: Lab 1.2 · 25 min The ten most expensive sessions Find the ten most expensive sessions and attribute their cost to steps, retries and context growth, then size a fix for each cause. D1_2_expensive_sessions.ipynb Cost per session, and the top ten 5 min Split each session: base, context growth, extra steps, retries 9 min Read the worst session step by step 5 min Three causes, three fixes and their size 6 min ✱ Stretch: What the agent would cost without its prefix cache

slides.title: Attribution and showback
slides.text: Session 3 Attribution and showback Attribute spend to team, application and environment through gateway keys and tags Produce a showback table that adds up to the invoice, with an unallocated row Compare two ways to allocate a cost that two teams share 03

slides.title: Allocate first, then optimise
slides.text: Attribution Allocate first, then optimise One invoice, five teams: until spend has an owner, nobody has a reason to lower it. An owner is a team, an application and an environment. The gateway is where that is recorded, because every request passes through it. At Mawj Shurooq in finance receives one PDF a month. The question she is asked is always "whose is it?", and the invoice has no column for that.

slides.title: A key says who is calling; a tag says what for
slides.text: Two mechanisms A key says who is calling; a tag says what for A gateway key Issued to one team, for one application, in one environment. Attribution costs nothing: it is the join of the log with the key register. A tag on the request Sent by the application: app=khulasa;caller=fasil. Finer than a key, and only as reliable as the code that sets it. Prefer keys. A key cannot be forgotten: a request without one is refused. A tag can be left out, and in October it was on 8% of the shared key's requests.

slides.title: The register says one team spent SAR 1,157. Three things are inside
slides.text: Lab 1.3 · what the register hides The register says one team spent SAR 1,157. Three things are inside On key-shared-legacy Requests SAR Khulasa, tagged 25,633 846.21 Another team's experiment on the large tier 1,115 239.90 No tag at all 2,161 70.48 What goes wrong. A key issued "for now" before keys per application existed. A team without a key borrowed it for a week, at SAR 0.215 a request against Khulasa's SAR 0.033.

slides.title: What nobody owns gets its own row
slides.text: Honest tables What nobody owns gets its own row Untagged requests on the shared key: SAR 70.48. A provider key outside the gateway : SAR 62.02, on the invoice and in no log. Together 1.6% of the invoice: small, visible, and somebody's job to shrink. Do not spread it Giving unallocated spend to the largest team, or to everyone by share, makes the table add up and removes the reason to fix the tags.

slides.title: The showback table adds up to the invoice
slides.text: Lab 1.3 · the result The showback table adds up to the invoice Contact-centre analytics SAR 4,318 · 52.4% Billing operations SAR 2,581 · 31.3% Customer care SAR 971 · 11.8% Network analytics SAR 240 · 2.9% Unallocated SAR 133 · 1.6% Contact-centre analytics leads because of the node lease, SAR 3,472, not because of Khulasa's tokens.

slides.title: Showback before chargeback
slides.text: A durable rule Showback before chargeback 1 · Showback each team sees its spend; no money moves → 2 · Corrections "that is not ours": tags and keys get fixed → 3 · Chargeback budgets are charged, from a table people trust Why the order. The first tables are wrong in ways only the teams can see. A team charged from a table it never saw disputes the table, not its spend.

slides.title: When one application calls another, there is no settled way to split the cost
slides.text: An open question When one application calls another, there is no settled way to split the cost Owner pays Khulasa's team pays for every summary, whoever asked. Simple; the owner carries other teams' demand. Caller pays The dispute agent's team pays for the summaries it requests. Fairer on demand; the owner loses a reason to make the service cheaper. At Mawj the rule moves SAR 46.05 between two teams and changes nothing in the total. State the rule on the table; show what the other one would give.

slides.title: The untagged 8%
slides.text: Checkpoint The untagged 8% 8% of the requests on a shared key carry no tag. Finance wants the showback table finished today. What do you do with their cost? Give it to the team that owns the key Spread it over all teams by their share of spend Leave it out, since it cannot be attributed Report it in an "unallocated" row and open the fix: a key per application

slides.title: A showback table from gateway keys
slides.text: Lab 1.3 · 25 min A showback table from gateway keys Tag spend by team, application and environment through gateway keys and produce a showback table that adds up to the invoice. D1_3_showback.ipynb Join the usage log to the key register 5 min Split the shared key by its tags 6 min Showback by team, application and environment 7 min Calls between applications: caller pays or owner pays 7 min ✱ Stretch: Spread the idle accelerator-hours by tokens and by requests

slides.title: Budgets and limits
slides.text: Session 4 Budgets and limits Write soft and hard budgets per application and environment Replay a spike and read which requests the gateway refused Choose between a budget and a rate limit for a given failure 04

slides.title: A soft budget tells someone; a hard budget refuses requests
slides.text: Budgets A soft budget tells someone; a hard budget refuses requests Soft level An alert when spend in the window crosses it. Nothing is refused. Hard level Every later request in the scope is refused until the window ends. Window and scope A day or a month; a key, an application, an environment, a team. Use both. Soft without hard is a message nobody must act on. Hard without soft is an outage with no warning.

slides.title: One budget for the whole gateway refused the wrong application
slides.text: 17 October, replayed One budget for the whole gateway refused the wrong application A tool outage made the dispute agent loop all afternoon. The gateway's single daily budget, SAR 260, was spent before the evening. Refused for the rest of the day: 474 requests of the care assistant, 261 of the agent, 216 of Khulasa. 229 customers of Anis got no answer in its busiest hours. The budget worked It stopped the spend. Its scope was the problem: the first application to overspend used up everyone's allowance.

slides.title: Levels come from the month's data, not from a round number
slides.text: Choosing the levels Levels come from the month's data, not from a round number Application Median day Highest normal day Hard Soft Anis 32.9 36.0 60 48 Khulasa 28.3 32.1 70 56 Fasil 79.9 106.6 165 132 SAR per day, October without the incident day. Hard at about one and a half times the highest normal day; soft at 80% of hard.

slides.title: The policy is a file you can review, replay and version
slides.text: Lab 1.4 · the policy The policy is a file you can review, replay and version {"window": "day", "budgets": [ {"scope": "app", "match": "anis", "soft_sar": 48, "hard_sar": 60}, {"scope": "app", "match": "khulasa", "soft_sar": 56, "hard_sar": 70}, {"scope": "app", "match": "fasil", "soft_sar": 132, "hard_sar": 165}], "rate_limits": [ {"scope": "app", "match": "fasil", "requests_per_minute": 12}]}

slides.title: With budgets per application the hard limit trips on the agent only
slides.text: Lab 1.4 · the result With budgets per application the hard limit trips on the agent only 39 min from soft alert to hard limit 961 agent requests refused, in 28 sessions 0 requests of Anis refused SAR 80 not spent that day A refusal is not free. Those 28 sessions were customers with a billing dispute. A hard limit needs a plan for them: hand the case to a person and say so.

slides.title: A rate limit acts in a minute; a budget acts in a day
slides.text: Limits A rate limit acts in a minute; a budget acts in a day Rate limit Requests or tokens per minute. For bursts and loops. At 12 requests a minute, twice the agent's busiest calm minute, the loop was slowed 2 hours 46 minutes before the budget ran out. Budget SAR per day or month. For the total. It does not notice a burst until the money is gone. The cheapest control of all was not at the gateway: a step budget in the agent (Lab 1.2) ends a loop at step 12.

slides.title: Three applications, one budget
slides.text: Checkpoint Three applications, one budget A gateway has one hard daily budget for all applications. An internal batch job doubles its volume. At the end of the afternoon the budget is reached. Who is refused in the evening? Only the batch job, since it caused the overspend Every application in the scope, the customer-facing one included Nobody: the gateway sends an alert and keeps serving The applications with the lowest priority first

slides.title: Soft and hard budgets, and a spike
slides.text: Lab 1.4 · 25 min Soft and hard budgets, and a spike Set soft and hard budgets per application on the gateway and trip the hard limit with the replayed spike of day 17, without refusing the care assistant. D1_4_budgets.ipynb Read the policy and replay a calm day 5 min Replay the spike under one global budget 5 min Budgets per application: soft and hard 8 min Trip the hard limit and read the gateway log 4 min A requests-per-minute limit for the agent 3 min ✱ Stretch: A budget per environment, so that staging cannot spend production money

slides.title: Where the money goes
slides.text: Day 1 · three things to keep Where the money goes Cost follows tokens, steps and utilisation Four kinds of token, billed failures, sessions that grow, and hours that are paid idle. Measure before optimising Reconcile with the invoice, split the bill into parts, size each fix. Allocate, then limit Keys per application, an unallocated row, showback first, budgets whose scope matches what they protect.

slides.title: Which request is on the bill?
slides.text: Review of Day 1 Which request is on the bill? The dispute agent sends a prompt of 20,000 tokens, 19,200 of them cached. The client times out after the provider has written 300 tokens. How is this attempt billed? Not at all, because no answer arrived 800 input tokens at the input price, 19,200 at the cached price, 300 at the output price 20,000 tokens at the input price and 300 at the output price 20,000 at the input price, 19,200 more at the cached price, 300 at the output price

slides.title: Own tasks, several settings
slides.text: Session 1 Own tasks, several settings Write a code grader for the care assistant and score six configurations Report quality, latency and cost per task, split by language Check supplied results against a live rerun of ten tasks 01

slides.title: Set the quality floor first, then cut cost
slides.text: The order of work Set the quality floor first, then cut cost 1 · Floor the owner states the lowest acceptable pass rate → 2 · Measure every candidate on your own tasks → 3 · Choose the cheapest candidate above the floor What goes wrong. Prices are compared first, a cheap configuration is chosen, and the floor is then set wherever that configuration happens to land.

slides.title: A leaderboard does not know your plans or your customers' Arabic
slides.text: Own-task evaluation A leaderboard does not know your plans or your customers' Arabic 100 labelled tasks per application , half in English and half in Arabic, each with the facts a right answer must hold. A grader in code : the facts are there and the answer is in the customer's language. Every candidate on the same tasks : three tiers, two reasoning settings, with tokens and latency recorded. One task of Anis كم سعر باقة Mawj 55 في الشهر وماذا تشمل؟ Must include: 55, 10. Language: Arabic.

slides.title: Six configurations on 100 tasks: quality, latency, cost
slides.text: Lab 2.1 · the care assistant Six configurations on 100 tasks: quality, latency, cost Tier Reasoning Pass rate Median latency SAR per task tier-s off 83% 1.1 s 0.0050 tier-s high 85% 3.6 s 0.0065 tier-m off 95% 1.8 s 0.0257 tier-m high 96% 6.7 s 0.0333 tier-l off 97% 2.8 s 0.1020 tier-l high 98% 10.6 s 0.1347

slides.title: The small tier passes in English and fails in Arabic
slides.text: The floor holds in each language The small tier passes in English and fails in Arabic tier-s · English 92% tier-s · Arabic 74% tier-m · English 96% tier-m · Arabic 94% Floor: 92% in each language. An average of 83% says "a bit low"; the split says who pays for it. Six in ten of Anis's customers write in Arabic.

slides.title: Reasoning is paid in output tokens and in seconds: buy it where it helps
slides.text: Reasoning settings Reasoning is paid in output tokens and in seconds: buy it where it helps Anis, a lookup High reasoning on the medium tier: 95% to 96%, one task. Cost up 30%, latency from 1.8 s to 6.7 s. Fasil, a decision in several steps High reasoning on the medium tier: 76% to 91%. Without it, no tier reaches the floor of 90%. A setting per application. The reasoning setting is a second dial beside the tier, and the right position differs by task.

slides.title: Three applications, three different answers
slides.text: The results table Three applications, three different answers Application Runs on Cheapest above the floor Finding Anis tier-m, off tier-m, off right-sized as one tier; routing is the next step Khulasa tier-m, off tier-s, off: 94%, SAR 0.0067 a task 79% cheaper per task at the floor Fasil tier-l, high tier-m, high: 91%, SAR 0.21 a task passes the floor by one task: not settled

slides.title: With 50 tasks per language, one task is two points
slides.text: How much a table can say With 50 tasks per language, one task is two points 94% and 92% differ by one task. Do not rank on that. A configuration exactly on the floor has passed once, on this sample. More tasks, repeated runs, or a paired comparison narrow it. The size of the saving says how much care it deserves. Report it this way "45 of 50 in Arabic, floor 46 of 50" is harder to misread than "90%".

slides.title: Supplied outputs are a recording: check a sample of it live
slides.text: Lab 2.1 · step 4 Supplied outputs are a recording: check a sample of it live 1 · Sample ten tasks, five per language → 2 · Rerun the same prompt against a live model → 3 · Compare the same grader; read each disagreement What it proves. That the prompt, the task and the grader work on a real model. A free hosted model is not the provider's tier, so it does not confirm the pass rates.

slides.title: 95% overall
slides.text: Checkpoint 95% overall A cheaper configuration scores 95% on 100 tasks: 50 of 50 in English, 45 of 50 in Arabic. The floor is 92% in each language. Most customers write in Arabic. What do you report? It passes: 95% is above the floor It passes if the floor for Arabic is lowered to 90% It fails and should be dropped from the table It fails the floor in Arabic; it is a candidate for English traffic only

slides.title: Routing and cascades
slides.text: Session 2 Routing and cascades Build a cascade with a quality check that needs no label and a fallback on errors Measure cost per successful outcome, failed first attempts included Write a router configuration that keeps the floor in Arabic and English 02

slides.title: Most requests do not need the tier that the hardest ones need
slides.text: Routing Most requests do not need the tier that the hardest ones need 5x the price of tier-m over tier-s 46 of 50 English tasks of Anis the small tier answers right 37 of 50 Arabic tasks it answers right One tier for everything pays the high price on every easy request. A router sends each request to the cheapest tier that can do it, and has to know which that is.

slides.title: Three ways to decide where a request goes
slides.text: Tiers, cascades and learned routers Three ways to decide where a request goes A rule before the call By something known up front: language, application, intent. Costs nothing. As good as the measurement behind it. A cascade Try the cheap tier, check the answer, escalate when the check fails. Pays twice for escalated requests. A learned router A small model predicts whether the cheap tier will do. Needs training data and its own evaluation. Lab 2.2 builds the first two. Whichever you use, it is judged the same way: cost per successful outcome at the floor.

slides.title: In production nobody tells the router that an answer was wrong
slides.text: The quality check of a cascade In production nobody tells the router that an answer was wrong What a check can see The call errored. The answer is empty. It is not in the language of the question. It hedges. It does not parse or breaks the schema. What it cannot see A fluent answer, in the right language, with the wrong fee. Seeing that needs the right answer, or a grader as good as the large tier. Measure the check too. On labelled tasks, count the failures it catches, the failures it lets through and the right answers it rejects.

slides.title: The check catches the visible failures; in Arabic most are not visible
slides.text: Lab 2.2 · the check, measured The check catches the visible failures; in Arabic most are not visible Failures of the small tier English Arabic Caught by the check, escalated 2 5 Let through: confident and wrong 2 8 Right answers rejected 0 0 A plain cascade therefore ends at 48 of 50 in English and 42 of 50 in Arabic: below the floor in the language of most customers.

slides.title: Failed first attempts are paid: divide all spend by the successes
slides.text: The number to choose by Failed first attempts are paid: divide all spend by the successes spend = sum(cost of EVERY attempt, the rejected ones too) successes = number of requests whose final answer was right cost_per_successful_outcome = spend / successes Two ways to fool yourself. Counting only the final attempt's cost flatters a cascade. Dividing by requests instead of successes flatters a tier that is cheap and wrong.

slides.title: The router that keeps both floors costs 38% less per success
slides.text: Lab 2.2 · the result The router that keeps both floors costs 38% less per success Policy English Arabic SAR per success Floor Always tier-s 92% 74% 0.0060 fails Always tier-m 96% 94% 0.0271 holds Cascade, s then m 96% 84% 0.0075 fails Cascade for English, Arabic direct to m 96% 94% 0.0167 holds 100 tasks of the care assistant, half in each language; supplied outputs.

slides.title: A fallback answers an outage; an escalation answers a doubt
slides.text: Two reasons to call a second model A fallback answers an outage; an escalation answers a doubt Fallback The first model errored or timed out after its retries. The gateway calls another model. Protects availability. Escalation The first model answered and the check rejected the answer. The router calls a stronger tier. Protects quality. A fallback target must have passed the same floor, or an outage quietly becomes a quality incident. Both are extra calls: both belong in cost per successful outcome.

slides.title: A cache belongs to one model: a switch in mid-conversation starts cold
slides.text: Cache cost of switching models A cache belongs to one model: a switch in mid-conversation starts cold 0.0047 SAR, a turn on tier-m with a warm cache 0.0247 SAR, the same turn right after a switch The tier that takes over has never seen the prompt: 7,600 input tokens at the full price, 5.3 times a warm turn. Route a conversation once, at its start, when you can. For an agent, a switch at step 20 repays the whole history.

slides.title: What the cascade costs
slides.text: Checkpoint What the cascade costs A cascade sends 100 requests to a tier at SAR 0.005 each. 20 fail the check and go to a tier at SAR 0.025. In the end 95 answers are right. What is the cost per successful outcome? SAR 0.0105: all 120 calls are paid, divided by 95 successes SAR 0.0100: total spend divided by 100 requests SAR 0.0095: 80 cheap calls and 20 dear ones, divided by 95 SAR 0.0150: the mean of the two tiers' prices

slides.title: Anis resends 8,400 tokens per request and none of them is cached
slides.text: The care assistant in October Anis resends 8,400 tokens per request and none of them is cached Part of the prompt Tokens Clock 14 Customer profile 27 Instructions and plan sheet 1,593 Policy sections 6,706 History and question 13 and up 99% of the prompt is the same text for every customer. The provider caches prefixes and the log shows 0 cached tokens for Anis. The parts are in the order above.

slides.title: A prompt is reused only as far as it is identical from its first token
slides.text: How a prefix cache works A prompt is reused only as far as it is identical from its first token From the start The cache compares prompts from token 1. The first difference ends the match. A minimum, in steps One large provider caches from 1,024 tokens and reports cached tokens in multiples of 128. For minutes An unused entry expires after about 5 minutes with two large providers; a use refreshes it. Longer lifetimes exist, at a price. Prices differ too. With one large provider a cached read costs a tenth of the input price and writing a 5-minute entry costs 1.25 times it.

slides.title: Three things break the shared prefix, and one is invisible in the template
slides.text: Lab 2.3 · the diagnosis Three things break the shared prefix, and one is invisible in the template Layout Two prompts are equal up to token What differs there Today 13 a clock with seconds in the first line Clock moved to the end 2 the customer's profile Profile after the policies 1,597 the policy sections, in another order each time Policy sections sorted 8,301 the two customers' profiles

slides.title: Stable first, variable last
slides.text: Prompt layout Stable first, variable last 1 · Same for everyone instructions, plan sheet, policy sections in a fixed order → 2 · Same in a conversation profile, then history → 3 · New each request the question, then the clock History is a prefix too. Turn 2 extends turn 1, so a conversation reuses its own earlier turns, if nothing that changes sits in front of them.

slides.title: The same words in another order: 82% cheaper and first token sooner
slides.text: Lab 2.3 · the result The same words in another order: 82% cheaper and first token sooner 0 → 98% of input tokens read from the cache 60.19 SAR for two busy hours before 10.73 SAR after -47% median time to first token, 578 to 307 ms 2,219 replayed requests of two evening hours through the cache model. Every request hits once the cache is warm.

slides.title: A cache pays when entries are reused before they expire
slides.text: The limits of the result A cache pays when entries are reused before they expire 45 requests, several minutes apart Hit rate SAR No cache 0% 1.214 5-minute entries, writes at 1.25 times input 16% 1.297 One-hour entries, writes at 2 times input 98% 0.282 Do not multiply the peak by the month. At night most entries expire between requests. With a write premium, a short-lived cache then costs more than no cache.

slides.title: Semantic caches and their risks
slides.text: Session 4 Semantic caches and their risks Measure hit rate and wrong-answer rate of a semantic cache at several thresholds Scope cache entries so that no answer crosses customers Write the isolation test that proves it 04

slides.title: A response cache skips the model: it serves an answer it gave before
slides.text: The other kind of cache A response cache skips the model: it serves an answer it gave before Prefix cache At the provider. The model still answers; it reads less. Cannot return a wrong answer. Exact response cache In your application. The same question, word for word, gets the stored answer. Semantic response cache A question that is close enough to a stored one gets its answer. "Close enough" is a threshold on similarity. A new kind of failure. A response cache can serve an answer that was right for another question, another day or another customer.

slides.title: A hit rate is half of a measurement
slides.text: Lab 2.4 · a cache with no scope A hit rate is half of a measurement Cache Hit rate Wrong answers, of all questions Another customer's answer Exact match 44.6% 20.5% 490 Semantic, threshold 0.80 74.8% 40.4% 490 Semantic, threshold 0.90 54.4% 24.2% 490 Semantic, threshold 0.95 45.7% 20.8% 490 2,400 labelled questions to the care assistant over a month.

slides.title: Two questions that differ in the one word that matters
slides.text: What a wrong hit looks like Two questions that differ in the one word that matters Askedبعد الانتقال والهاتف الثابت في الطائف: لا توجد بيانات. ماذا أفعل؟ Served from the cacheThe answer stored for: بعد الانتقال والهاتف الثابت في الطائف: رمز الخطأ 31. ماذا أفعل؟ Same device, same city, same wording; one says "no data", the other "error code 31". At threshold 0.80 they are close enough. Plans that differ by a number and "activate" against "deactivate" fail the same way.

slides.title: No threshold stops one customer's answer reaching another
slides.text: Isolation between customers No threshold stops one customer's answer reaching another "What is my current balance?" from two customers is the same question: similarity 1, and an exact match too. The answers differ because the data differs, not the words. 490 answers crossed at every threshold, and with the exact cache. This is a disclosure A balance or a bill shown to the wrong person is personal data disclosed. It is an incident to report to the data protection officer, not a quality metric.

slides.title: Scope every entry by whose data produced it, and test that nothing crosses
slides.text: Lab 2.4 · the fix and its test Scope every entry by whose data produced it, and test that nothing crosses def scope_of(q): # known when the answer is written return f"customer:{q['customer']}" if q["used_customer_data"] else "public" def test_no_answer_crosses_customers(served): assert served.crossed.sum() == 0 An answer that read the customer's account lives in that customer's partition; everything else is shared. The test needs no labels. It fails on the unscoped cache and passes on the scoped one, at every threshold.

slides.title: With isolation fixed, the threshold trades hits for wrong answers
slides.text: Lab 2.4 · the scoped cache With isolation fixed, the threshold trades hits for wrong answers Scoped cache, threshold Hit rate Wrong answers, of all questions Crossed 0.80 54.7% 20.0% 0 0.90 34.3% 3.8% 0 0.95 25.6% 0.3% 0 With at most 1% wrong answers allowed, 0.95 is the choice: a quarter of the questions served without the model, about SAR 233 of Anis's SAR 911 a month.

slides.title: A cached answer is right until the world changes
slides.text: Staleness A cached answer is right until the world changes On day 15 the price of one plan changed. At 0.95 the cache served the old price twice, on days 23 and 25. A 3-day lifetime on every entry removes both, and cuts the hit rate from 25.6% to 9.0%. Better: tie entries to the version of what they were built from, and drop them when it changes. Three questions for any cache Whose data is in the entry? How long is it true? What tells the cache that it no longer is?

slides.title: The balance of another customer
slides.text: Checkpoint The balance of another customer A semantic cache at threshold 0.90 served one customer the account balance of another. The team proposes to raise the threshold to 0.97. What do you answer? Agreed: at 0.97 only near-identical questions match It will not help: partition entries by customer when the answer used account data, and test it Use a stronger embedding model so the two questions separate Give the entries a lifetime of one hour

slides.title: Work that can wait costs half
slides.text: Batch tiers Work that can wait costs half You submit a file of requests; the provider answers them when it has spare capacity. The published terms of the large providers: half the price, results within 24 hours. No streaming and no conversation: each request stands alone and is matched to its answer by an identifier you set. At Mawj Khulasa summarises a call after it has ended. Nobody is waiting on the line. It has run on the interactive tier since its first day.

slides.text: Lab 3.2 · steps 1 and 2 The same month on the batch tier: half, and the failed attempts disappear 1,132 SAR, 26,000 calls on the interactive tier, in-Kingdom 561 SAR, the same calls on the batch tier 546 failed interactive attempts that were billed: SAR 10 A batch has no client waiting, so no client times out and pays for an answer it never read.

slides.title: The promise is a ceiling; what you plan with is a distribution
slides.text: What "within 24 hours" means The promise is a ceiling; what you plan with is a distribution 38 min median completion of a batch 2 h 43 95th percentile 6 h 49 the longest of the month What goes wrong. A team tests one batch, sees it finish in half an hour and promises that to the business. One batch in twenty takes more than five times as long.

B · The summary job triples Three times the calls, a larger pilot, a node leased twelve hours a night. C · The dispute agent rolls out Twice the disputes, most of them on the cheaper configuration. You submit a public repository: the notebook, the measured results and the two-page review. You defend it in ten minutes : you recompute one savings figure the assessor picks and explain one routing decision.

slides.title: The total on page one
slides.text: Checkpoint The total on page one A draft review lists a prompt layout change (82% off the assistant's spend), a router (38% off) and a semantic cache (25% off), each measured alone on the same assistant, and promises finance the three together. What do you change? Measure the three applied together in shipping order, or promise only the first Nothing: the three percentages add up to the total saving Report the average of the three, 48% Keep the largest and delete the other two from the review

slides.title: Host or buy, and report
slides.text: Day 3 · three things to keep Host or buy, and report Placement, floor, then price The register first. A node is a question of utilisation against the best allowed alternative. The outcome is the unit Cost per resolved dispute, with the failures and the people who clean up after them. Two pages that ask for a decision Three measured options, one refusal, energy beside cost, and what was not measured.

slides.title: Your review, defended
slides.text: Capstone day Your review, defended An unseen month, a repository with measured results, two pages, and ten minutes in which you recompute one figure while the assessor watches. Generate your scenario and read labs/capstone/README.md before you start. Reconcile the cost model with the invoice first: no other number can be trusted before that. Rehearse the recomputation once, with a timer.

slides.title: The rubric
slides.text: How presentations are scored The rubric Cost model accuracy 20% Routing evaluation 25% Caching evidence 20% Hosting analysis 20% Review quality 15% Every figure in the review is printed by a cell of the notebook. A saving without a measurement is a plan, not a result.

slides.title: 10 minutes for each defence
slides.text: Format 10 minutes for each defence 1 · The month · 2 minutes Three numbers and the decision you ask for. Your review is on the screen. 2 · One figure, live · 5 minutes The assessor picks a savings figure. You recompute it from the log and say what it includes and what it leaves out. 3 · One routing decision · 3 minutes The assessor selects it. Which requests go where, what the check misses, what would change your mind. No assistant during the defence. Peer feedback after each one: a strength, a question and a suggestion.
